paragraphs.title: The Psalm’s Heading and the Cry of the Persecuted

easy.explanation: He begins, “My God, my God,” calling directly upon God.
easy.q: To whom does the speaker cry?

answers: In the daytime and in the night season
easy.explanation: He says he cries “in the daytime” and “in the night season.”
easy.q: When does the speaker cry to God?

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “thou hearest not.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say God has not done?

medium.explanation: Calling in both daytime and nighttime shows persistence and distress.
medium.q: What does the repeated mention of day and night emphasize?

medium.explanation: The question shows that the speaker feels abandoned and far from help.
medium.q: What feeling is expressed in “why hast thou forsaken me”?

medium.explanation: The speaker feels that deliverance is distant from him.
medium.q: What does “far from helping me” mean in context?

answers: The speaker cries continually but senses no answer
The speaker celebrates without an audience
challenge.explanation: He calls to God day and night, yet says that God does not answer.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in these opening verses?

challenge.explanation: “Roaring” portrays the intensity of the speaker’s anguished prayer.
challenge.q: What does “the words of my roaring” suggest?

answers: He is isolated, distressed, and seeking divine help
He is confident that his enemies are defeated
He is preparing a public feast
challenge.explanation: The opening combines abandonment, unanswered prayer, and a desperate appeal to God.
challenge.q: How does the opening establish the speaker’s condition?

paragraphs.title: God’s Holiness and the Ancestors’ Deliverance

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “thou art holy.”
easy.q: How is God described?

easy.explanation: The fathers trusted in God and depended on Him.
easy.q: In whom did the fathers trust?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “They cried unto thee, and were delivered.”
easy.q: What happened when the fathers cried unto God?

medium.explanation: He recalls that the fathers trusted, cried, and were delivered.
medium.q: What does the speaker remember to strengthen his faith?

answers: They trusted, cried, and were delivered
medium.explanation: The verses connect trust and prayer with God’s deliverance.
medium.q: What sequence is repeated about the fathers?

answers: God is present amid Israel’s praises
medium.explanation: The phrase pictures God as dwelling among the praises of His people.
medium.q: What does “thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel” suggest?

challenge.explanation: Their deliverance gives him a reason to continue trusting God.
challenge.q: Why does the speaker mention the fathers after describing his distress?

answers: He feels unanswered, while the fathers were delivered
He is celebrating, while they are mourning
He is strong, while they are victorious
challenge.explanation: The speaker feels abandoned even though the fathers trusted and escaped.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the speaker and the fathers?

answers: Those who trusted God were not disappointed
challenge.explanation: The phrase declares that the trusting fathers were not put to shame.
challenge.q: What does “were not confounded” emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Humiliation, Mockery, and Remembered Divine Support

easy.explanation: He says, “I am a worm, and no man.”
easy.q: How does the speaker describe himself?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “All they that see me laugh me to scorn.”
easy.q: What do those who see him do?

answers: From the beginning of the battle
easy.explanation: He says that God took him out of the womb and made him hope.
easy.q: From when does the speaker remember God’s care?

answers: It proves that he has won
medium.explanation: The laughter and scorn deepen his sense of shame and weakness.
medium.q: How does the mockery affect the speaker’s condition?

answers: To explain the division of garments
medium.explanation: He remembers that God supported him from the womb and infancy.
medium.q: Why does the speaker recall God’s care from birth?

answers: God gave him confidence and dependence from infancy
medium.explanation: The phrase shows that his earliest hope was placed in God.
medium.q: What does “thou didst make me hope” mean?

answers: Human contempt is set against divine support
Joy is set against a feast
Enemies are set against the fathers
challenge.explanation: People despise him, but he remembers that God has supported him since birth.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the mockers and God’s past care?

answers: He fears being left alone in trouble
He is thanking God for victory
challenge.explanation: He asks for God’s nearness because trouble is near and no helper is present.
challenge.q: What does “Be not far from me” reveal?

answers: Past support becomes the basis for a present plea
The speaker forgets his past and mentions only enemies
The speaker describes only the future
challenge.explanation: He remembers God’s care from birth and asks for that care again.
challenge.q: How do these verses connect past and present?

paragraphs.title: Encircling Enemies and the Body’s Collapse

easy.explanation: The passage compares the enemies to bulls, a ravening lion, and dogs.
easy.q: What animals represent the enemies?

answers: It is dried up like a potsherd
It is increasing like a tree
It is firm like a mountain
easy.explanation: He says, “My strength is dried up like a potsherd.”
easy.q: How does the speaker describe his strength?

answers: They part them and cast lots
easy.explanation: They divide his garments and cast lots for his vesture.
easy.q: What do the enemies do with his garments?

answers: A sense of danger surrounding him
medium.explanation: The animal images portray enemies pressing in from every side.
medium.q: What effect is created by the images of bulls, lions, and dogs?

answers: It is collapsing and losing strength
It feels no pain or weakness
medium.explanation: His bones are out of joint, his heart melts, and his strength dries up.
medium.q: How is the speaker’s body portrayed?

answers: His whole body and physical condition
medium.explanation: Mentioning all his bones emphasizes the extent of his bodily distress.
medium.q: What does “all my bones” refer to in context?

answers: It makes the enemies seem to regard his fate as already decided
It shows that the speaker is celebrating
challenge.explanation: The enemies act as though they already possess his belongings and victory is theirs.
challenge.q: How does the division of the garments intensify the danger?

answers: External threats are joined to inner physical collapse
The body is unaffected by the enemies
challenge.explanation: The surrounding enemies accompany vivid descriptions of physical weakness.
challenge.q: What relationship exists between the animals and the bodily images?

answers: Many different forms of threat and surrounding danger
A change from enemies to friends
A transition from prayer to thanksgiving
challenge.explanation: The changing animal images build a picture of numerous and frightening attackers.
challenge.q: What does the movement from bulls to the lion to dogs emphasize?

easy.explanation: He directly asks the LORD to help and deliver him.
easy.q: From whom does the speaker seek deliverance?

answers: The sword, the dog, and the lion
easy.explanation: He mentions the sword, the power of the dog, and the lion’s mouth.
easy.q: From what dangers does he ask to be saved?

easy.explanation: He says, “O my strength, haste thee to help me.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God to do quickly?

answers: Trouble is near and there is no helper
The speaker is preparing a feast
medium.explanation: The earlier verses say that trouble is near and no one else can help.
medium.q: Why is the plea urgent?

answers: They mention the dog, lion, and threatening beasts again
medium.explanation: The speaker gathers the earlier animal images into a direct request for rescue.
medium.q: How do these verses repeat earlier images?

answers: God is the speaker’s source of strength
medium.explanation: Calling God “my strength” shows dependence upon Him.
medium.q: What does “my strength” indicate about God?

answers: He remains dependent on God’s nearness
He is speaking to his enemies
challenge.explanation: Even in danger, he asks God to stay near and act quickly.
challenge.q: What does “Be not thou far from me” reveal about the speaker?

answers: He is asking for the preservation of his life
challenge.explanation: The terms refer to his vulnerable life and person, which he asks God to save.
challenge.q: Why does he ask God to deliver his soul and his darling?

answers: The psalm moves from describing danger to directly requesting rescue
It moves from thanksgiving to mockery
It moves from birth to the fathers
challenge.explanation: After portraying the threats, the speaker urgently appeals to God for deliverance.
challenge.q: What major movement occurs in these verses?

paragraphs.title: Public Praise and Fulfillment of the Vow

easy.explanation: He says, “I will declare thy name unto my brethren.”
easy.q: What does the speaker promise to declare?

answers: Those who fear the LORD and all Israel
easy.explanation: He calls on those who fear the LORD, the seed of Jacob, and Israel.
easy.q: Who is called to praise and glorify the LORD?

answers: Eat, be satisfied, and praise the LORD
easy.explanation: The meek shall eat, be satisfied, and praise the LORD.
easy.q: What shall the meek do?

answers: Deliverance leads to testimony and worship in the congregation
Deliverance causes the speaker to hide
medium.explanation: The speaker responds to God’s help by declaring His name and praising Him publicly.
medium.q: What is the connection between deliverance and public praise?

answers: He does not despise them and hears their cry
He hides His face from them
medium.explanation: The passage says God has not despised or abhorred the afflicted and heard him when he cried.
medium.q: How does God treat the afflicted?

answers: Promises or commitments made to God
medium.explanation: The speaker promises to pay his vows before those who fear God.
medium.q: What are “my vows”?

answers: He has moved from distressed petitioner to public witness
He has changed from savior to enemy
He has changed from king to mocker
challenge.explanation: He now declares God’s name, praises Him, and fulfills his vows before the congregation.
challenge.q: How has the speaker’s role changed from the beginning?

answers: They eat, are satisfied, and praise the LORD
challenge.explanation: The passage connects their satisfaction with praise and seeking the LORD.
challenge.q: What blessing is associated with the meek?

answers: The speaker praises God in the congregation and calls others to worship
He does not want anyone to know of his deliverance
He speaks only to his enemies
challenge.explanation: His testimony takes place among the congregation and invites Israel to glorify God.
challenge.q: Why is the thanksgiving not private?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “For the kingdom is the LORD’S.”
easy.q: To whom does the kingdom belong?

answers: All the ends of the world
easy.explanation: The passage says that all the ends of the world shall remember and turn to Him.
easy.q: Who shall remember and turn unto the LORD?

easy.explanation: The nations are described as worshipping before Him.
easy.q: What shall the kindreds of the nations do?

answers: It leads the nations to recognize God’s kingship
It causes the nations to fight
medium.explanation: The vision includes the ends of the world and all the kindreds of the nations.
medium.q: How does salvation expand beyond the individual speaker?

answers: The nations remember, turn, and worship
The nations forget, flee, and mock
The nations eat, sleep, and hide
medium.explanation: The verse presents remembrance, turning to the LORD, and worship as a progression.
medium.q: What sequence appears in verse 27?

answers: The farthest parts of the earth
medium.explanation: The expression refers broadly to all distant regions of the world.
medium.q: What does “the ends of the world” mean?

answers: Recognition of God expands from the congregation to the whole world
challenge.explanation: The praise that began among God’s people broadens into universal worship.
challenge.q: What idea emerges as the passage moves from Israel to the nations?

answers: His kingship is not limited to Israel
God belongs only to the nations
The nations refuse to acknowledge Him
challenge.explanation: Calling Him governor among the nations presents His authority as universal.
challenge.q: What does God’s rule among the nations emphasize?

answers: The deliverance becomes a sign leading to worldwide recognition of God
The deliverance leads to the casting of lots
challenge.explanation: The personal salvation develops into a vision of the nations turning to and worshipping God.
challenge.q: How are these verses connected to the earlier deliverance?

paragraphs.title: Passing the Story to Future Generations

easy.explanation: The verse says, “A seed shall serve him.”
easy.q: What will the future seed do?

easy.explanation: They shall declare His righteousness to a people yet to be born.
easy.q: What will future generations declare?

answers: To a people that shall be born
easy.explanation: The passage speaks of declaring God’s righteousness to a future people.
easy.q: To whom will the message be declared?

answers: The account of God’s righteousness and deeds
medium.explanation: Future generations will declare His righteousness and what He has done.
medium.q: What is passed from one generation to another?

answers: Future generations will both serve Him and testify about Him
They will testify but not serve
They will serve but hide His works
medium.explanation: The verses combine service to God with active proclamation of His righteousness.
medium.q: What connection exists between serving God and declaring His deeds?

medium.explanation: It refers to people who will live in generations still to come.
medium.q: What does “a people that shall be born” refer to?

answers: It moves from personal distress to testimony for future generations
It moves from praise to mockery
It moves from kingship to unbelief
challenge.explanation: The psalm ends with God’s righteousness being proclaimed beyond the speaker’s own lifetime.
challenge.q: How does the ending complete the movement of the psalm?

answers: Future generations will actively preserve the testimony
challenge.explanation: The wording presents future people as active participants in passing on the message.
challenge.q: What does “They shall come, and shall declare” suggest?

answers: Future generations will remember His faithful and saving deeds
They will focus only on the enemies’ power
They will speak only about the speaker’s suffering
challenge.explanation: The conclusion directs the lasting testimony toward God’s righteousness and what He has done.
challenge.q: Why is the final message about God’s righteousness?
